title: Alerts that page and traces that connect
summary: Alert on symptoms with a for: window instead of noisy thresholds, and follow one message from producer to consumer with W3C traceparent headers and correlation ids.

steps.title: Good alerts, noisy alerts
body: An alert that pages must mean **users are hurt or soon will be, and a human can act now**. Everything else is a ticket
or a dashboard.
| Page (wake someone up) | Ticket (next working day) | Dashboard only |
| lag in **time** above the SLO and still growing for 10 min | DLQ depth > 0 and rising | a single rebalance |
| `UnderMinIsrPartitionCount` > 0 (writes failing) | `UnderReplicatedPartitions` > 0 for 30 min | CPU at 70% |
| `OfflinePartitionsCount` > 0 | broker disk > 75% | queue depth during a known nightly batch |
| RabbitMQ memory or disk alarm (publishers blocked) | redelivery rate > 5% for an hour | consumer count changes during a deploy |
| broker disk > 90% | certificate expiry in 14 days | |
Rules that keep alerts quiet and useful:
- **Symptoms over causes**: "invoices are late" pages; "CPU high" does not.
- A **`for:` window**: the condition must hold for several minutes, so a burst that drains on its own never pages.
- **Growth, not size**: a large lag that shrinks is a recovering system. Combine a threshold with "still growing".
- Every page links a **runbook** and has an owner; if an alert has fired ten times without action, delete or fix it.

items: billing lag = 14 minutes of orders and growing for 10 minutes
One consumer group rebalanced during a deploy
Queue depth spikes to 50 000 at the 02:00 batch and drains by 02:20
explain: Page only for what hurts users now and needs a human now. The DLQ and disk at 78% need work but not at 3 am; a
batch spike that drains itself and a deploy rebalance are normal operation.

steps.title: Evaluate a lag alert with a for: window
prompt: Implement the state machine Prometheus uses for an alert rule, for one lag series.
Write `List<string> Evaluate(List<(long TimeSec, long Lag)> samples, long threshold, long forSec)`.
- The **condition** at a sample is true when `Lag > threshold` **and** there is a previous sample **and**
`Lag >= previous Lag` (still growing or flat).
- When the condition becomes true the alert is `pending` (remember the time). When it has been true continuously
for at least `forSec` (`t - pendingSince >= forSec`, possibly at the same sample) it is `firing`.
- When the condition is false: a firing alert becomes `resolved`; a pending one is `cleared`; then it starts over.
- Return the transitions as `"t={time} pending"`, `"t={time} firing"`, `"t={time} resolved"`, `"t={time} cleared"`.
starter: List<string> Evaluate(List<(long TimeSec, long Lag)> samples, long threshold, long forSec)
solution: List<string> Evaluate(List<(long TimeSec, long Lag)> samples, long threshold, long forSec)
var condition = lag > threshold && previous is long p && lag >= p;
else if (since is not null) result.Add($"t={t} cleared");
hints: Keep three pieces of state: the previous lag, the time the condition became true (`long?`) and whether it is firing.
`previous is long p && lag >= p` is false for the first sample.
Check for firing right after setting pending, so `forSec = 0` fires on the same sample.

Dojo.Eq("for: 0 fires at once; flat counts as growing", new List<string> { "t=60 pending", "t=60 firing" },

steps.prompt: Complete the Prometheus rule (lag from `kafka_exporter`). Lag is a gauge, not a counter.
explain: `sum by` adds the partitions of a group. `deriv` gives the slope of a **gauge**; `rate` is only for counters, which
only go up. `for: 10m` keeps a short burst from paging, and every paging rule links its runbook.

steps.title: Tracing through a broker
body: An HTTP call carries its trace context in the `traceparent` header; a message must carry it **in its own headers**,
or the trace ends at the producer.
```text
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
version  trace-id (32 hex, whole flow)  parent span id   flags (01 = sampled)
(16 hex)
orders-api  [POST /orders]--[send orders]  -- Kafka header traceparent -->  billing [process orders]--[INSERT invoice]
same trace-id all the way; the consumer span's parent is the producer span
```csharp
static readonly ActivitySource Source = new("Shop.Orders");
// producer
using var activity = Source.StartActivity("send orders", ActivityKind.Producer);
var headers = new Headers();
if (activity is not null) headers.Add("traceparent", Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(activity.Id!));   // W3C format by default
await producer.ProduceAsync("orders", new Message<string, string> { Key = orderId, Value = json, Headers = headers });
// consumer
ActivityContext parent = default;
if (cr.Message.Headers.TryGetLastBytes("traceparent", out var raw))
ActivityContext.TryParse(Encoding.ASCII.GetString(raw), null, out parent);
using var span = Source.StartActivity("process orders", ActivityKind.Consumer, parent);
span?.SetTag("messaging.system", "kafka");
span?.SetTag("messaging.destination.name", "orders");
span?.SetTag("messaging.consumer.group.name", "billing");
- RabbitMQ.Client 7 creates these activities and propagates `traceparent` in message headers itself; listen to them
with OpenTelemetry's `.AddSource("RabbitMQ.Client.*")`. For Confluent.Kafka, add headers yourself as above (or use
the OpenTelemetry contrib instrumentation package).
- A **correlation id** is the business-level twin: carry `orderId` (or a `CorrelationId` property / header) on every
message and put it in every log line via a logging scope, so you can search all services for one order even where
tracing is sampled out.

explain: Field 1 is the trace id, field 2 the parent span id, field 3 the flags; bit 0 of the flags is "sampled". .NET prints

steps.title: Continue the trace
prompt: A consumer must continue the producer's trace, or start a new one when the header is missing or broken.
- `string? ChildTraceparent(string? incoming, string newSpanId)`: if `incoming` is a valid version-00 `traceparent`,
return it with the parent span id replaced by `newSpanId` (same trace id, same flags); otherwise `null` (the caller
starts a new trace). Valid means: 4 fields separated by `-`; version `00`; a trace id of 32 and a span id of 16
**lowercase** hex characters, neither all zeros; flags of 2 lowercase hex characters.
- `bool Sampled(string traceparent)`: bit 0 of the flags (assume a valid header).
solution: bool IsHex(string s, int length) => s.Length == length && s.All(c => c is >= '0' and <= '9' or >= 'a' and <= 'f');
hints: A helper `bool IsHex(string s, int length)` that checks the length and `c is >= '0' and <= '9' or >= 'a' and <= 'f'` for every character.
Split on `-`, check each field, then rebuild the string with the new span id in field 2.
template: Dojo.Eq("keeps trace id and flags, new parent", "00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-53995c3f42cd8ad8-01",
Dojo.Eq("an all-zero trace id is invalid", (string?)null, ChildTraceparent("00-00000000000000000000000000000000-00f067aa0ba902b7-01", "53995c3f42cd8ad8"));
Dojo.Eq("an all-zero span id is invalid", (string?)null, ChildTraceparent("00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-0000000000000000-01", "53995c3f42cd8ad8"));

steps.prompt: A billing consumer reads 50 messages at once and writes them in **one** database batch. Each message carries a different `traceparent`. How should the processing span relate to the 50 producer spans?
options: One `process` span with a **link** to each message's span context, as the OpenTelemetry messaging conventions describe for batches
Make the first message's span the parent and ignore the other 49
Start 50 spans, all in the same new trace
Copy the 50 trace ids into one tag
explain: A span has one parent but any number of **links**. For batch processing the conventions say: one span for the batch,
linked to every message it processed, so each producer's trace still leads to the batch that handled it

steps.title: End-to-end latency from the logs
prompt: Use the traces to answer "how late are our messages, and did any get lost?".
Write `List<string> EndToEnd(string[] logLines, long slowMs)`. Each line is `"{timeMs} {service} {publish|consume} traceparent={value}"`.
- Lines whose `traceparent` is not valid (the rules of the previous step) are counted, not used.
- Group the valid lines by **trace id**, in order of first appearance. For each trace (use the first 8 characters of the
trace id as its name):
- with a publish and a consume line: latency = first consume time - first publish time →
`"{id8}: {latency} ms"`, plus `" SLOW"` when latency > `slowMs`;
- with a publish but no consume: `"{id8}: published, never consumed"`;
- with a consume but no publish: `"{id8}: consumed, publish not seen"`.
- If any lines were invalid, add `"invalid traceparent lines: {n}"` at the end.
solution: bool IsHex(string s, int length) => s.Length == length && s.All(c => c is >= '0' and <= '9' or >= 'a' and <= 'f');
var hasP = published.TryGetValue(id, out var p);
var hasC = consumed.TryGetValue(id, out var c);
if (hasP && hasC) result.Add($"{name}: {c - p} ms" + (c - p > slowMs ? " SLOW" : ""));
else if (hasP) result.Add($"{name}: published, never consumed");
else result.Add($"{name}: consumed, publish not seen");
hints: Reuse your validation from the previous step as a helper method.
Keep a list of trace ids in first-seen order and two dictionaries (first publish time, first consume time); `TryAdd` keeps the first.
template: Dojo.Eq("latency per trace, the lost one and the broken header", new List<string>
Dojo.Eq("a consume without its publish", new List<string> { "abcdef01: consumed, publish not seen" },
Dojo.Eq("nothing logged", new List<string>(), EndToEnd(new string[0], 1000));
